section_summary: This section opens with a translated article reproducing Prince Fumimaro Konoe’s February 1945 memorial to the Emperor and recounting the military police investigation that followed. A September 1949 memorandum urges the United States to outlaw the Japanese Communist Party before withdrawal. Two later despatches transmit a translated party pamphlet on gaining power, peace terms and religion, and an intelligence report on Communist peace campaigns.

subfiles.title: Prince Konoe's Memorial to the Throne
subfiles.doc_type: ATIS special translation of article and reproduced memorial
subfiles.about: Publishes Prince Konoe's February 1945 warning that prolonging the war risked Communist revolution and recounts the subsequent military police investigation.
subfiles.summary: The memorial argues that Soviet ambitions, domestic unrest and reformist factions within the Japanese army made Communist revolution a growing danger, and urges an early end to the war after purging the army faction that opposed it. The accompanying article describes late-war military planning, Konoe's audience with the Emperor and the military police pursuit of people thought to know the memorial's contents.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Communist problem in Japan
subfiles.about: Bishop urges outlawing the Communist Party before United States forces leave Japan.
subfiles.summary: Urges destroying and outlawing the Communist organization before withdrawal.

subfiles.title: Communist Pamphlet on Feasibility of Communism under the Occupation
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a translated Communist pamphlet and highlights its proposals for a peace treaty and the return of islands.
subfiles.summary: Sebald summarizes the pamphlet's criticism of separate peace, its nine peace terms and its ambiguous territorial demand, which might cover the Ryukyus, Bonins or Kurils.

subfiles.title: Is It Possible to Establish a CP Regime Under the Occupation?
subfiles.from: Tokushima Prefectural Committee of the Japan Communist Party
subfiles.about: Explains the party's proposed path to power, peace terms and views on religion in question-and-answer form.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet argues that occupation policy permits Communist political activity and that the party seeks power through elections, mass movements and a democratic people's front rather than an armed uprising. It advocates a prompt treaty with all Allied powers, full sovereignty, troop withdrawal and the return of islands claimed on ethnic and historical grounds. A supplement promises religious freedom while explaining the party's Marxist view of religion.

subfiles.title: Communist Peace Movement in Japan
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits an intelligence report on the Japanese Communist peace movement.
subfiles.summary: Transmits ten copies of a report and notes possible effects on Japanese reactions to treaty terms.

subfiles.title: Communist Peace Movement in Japan
subfiles.about: Surveys Communist-sponsored peace societies, rallies, directives and the October 1949 Peace Protection Day.
subfiles.summary: The report traces local peace societies and rallies across Japan, describes a party directive tying workplace and local grievances to peace agitation, and recounts October 2 events in Tokyo and Yokohama. It interprets the campaign as Soviet-aligned propaganda aimed at shaping attitudes toward a peace treaty. Its assessment is that attendance and immediate results were limited, while the eventual effect remained uncertain.

subfiles.title: Agencies to Which CIS Furnished Intelligence
subfiles.about: Charts distribution of CIS special intelligence from September 1 to October 1, 1949.
subfiles.summary: Lists receiving agencies and a grand total of 700 intelligence items.
